title: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The ease of crossing two species often differs greatly depending on which species is the father and which the mother, showing that crossing capacity depends on imperceptible differences confined to the reproductive system.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: There is often the widest possible difference in the facility of making reciprocal crosses.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VIII, “Hybridism”; section “Laws governing the sterility of hybrids”. Scope: plants and animals, including seaweeds (Fucus) and close varieties

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch08-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.77

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Reciprocal crossing is a direct controlled comparison with strong discriminating power. Numerous public datasets allow immediate resolution of the phenomenon, though not exhaustive prevalence estimation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare fertilization, offspring number, and viability in both reciprocal directions for the same species pairs. Large repeatable direction effects support the claim; symmetry across well-powered pairs opposes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Cross records are decentralized and taxonomically uneven.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.96
data existence: 0.73
discriminating power: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison of reciprocal directions is simple and highly discriminating when both directions were published separately. The most convenient open fly compilation often folds those directions into one index, so recovering the asymmetry means going back to papers. That is a feasible partial test, not a ready analysis of plants and animals at the stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For species pairs crossed in both directions, compare offspring production with the sexes reversed. Frequent large asymmetries support the claim; consistently equal reciprocal success would refute the statement that the difference is often very wide.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Major compilations often average or sum reciprocal outcomes, erasing the contrast.

A difference in success does not by itself locate the cause in an imperceptible reproductive detail.

Direction-specific tables for plants, Fucus, and vertebrates are scattered.
